I ranked impl-2 first, impl-3 second and impl-1 third. All three pass their own test suites: impl-1 45 tests, impl-2 46, impl-3 34.

impl-2 is the most correct and most idiomatic:
- It turns on Model::shouldBeStrict, and the listing runs in 3 queries.
- A hidden is_active=0 input keeps the unchecked checkbox state after a failed submit (verified by probe). It is the only implementation that does.
- It ships a custom pagination view that works without Tailwind.
- Field errors go through an accessible x-form.error component.
- Search escapes LIKE wildcards.
- Its tests are the strongest of the three.
- Weak points: the admin enters price in EUR and it is converted to cents, and a typed slug is silently rewritten. Both are scope creep rather than defects.

impl-3 is clean and Blade-idiomatic:
- The shared form is a component, with an x-field wrapper using slots and an x-badge component.
- It eager-loads correctly: 4 queries on the listing.
- Against it: search doesn't escape wildcards (?q=% matches everything), and the checkbox state is lost after a failed submit.
- Its filter scope takes one catch-all array, and its tests are thinner and use a foreach loop where a Pest dataset would fit.

impl-1 has very good scopes, form components and tests, but its public catalogue has a real N+1. The product card reads category without eager loading: 15 queries for 12 products, which also breaks the 'no queries in views' rule. It also loses the checkbox state, as impl-3 does, and puts the default Tailwind pagination on an unstyled page.

impl-1 and impl-3 were close. The N+1 on the main public page was the deciding bug.

v.rationale:
impl-2 is the most correct and idiomatic. It is the only one that keeps an unticked checkbox's state after a failed submit (it uses a hidden input). It is also the only one that escapes search wildcards in a way that works on SQLite, lets admins enter the price in euros, and uses strict mode with eager loading. It has the strongest tests. Its remaining issues are cosmetic: a redundant slug error, and invalid filters redirecting away from the page.

impl-3 is clean and simple, with good component use (an x-field wrapper with a slot, a form component). But it has the checkbox old-input bug, unescaped LIKE wildcards, and a price field entered in cents.

impl-1 has good structure and tests, but more real bugs. The public catalogue has an N+1 query problem (15 queries per page), and the wildcard escaping does not work on SQLite, which its test fails to catch because it only checks that nothing matches. It shares the checkbox bug, puts setRelation logic in a view, and relies on the default Tailwind pagination view patched with CSS.

v.rationale:
I ran each suite and probed all three. They passed their own suites (20, 26 and 30 tests) and behaved the same in my probes for null fields, slug collisions, titles made only of symbols, unicode titles, invalid tags, keeping published_at, and other users' posts being isolated. Because they are so close, the ranking comes down to small routing and idiom differences.

impl-2 ranks first. It uses apiResource, so both PUT and PATCH work, and route binding uses the slug. It reads the status filter with $request->enum, writes update rules as 'sometimes','required', and uses ??= in the observer. Its flaws are small: postAttributes() is duplicated in two requests, and it uses getRouteKeyName() instead of the #[RouteKey] attribute.

impl-3 ranks second. It has the most thorough tests, an elegant route-level ->can() check, and nullable when() scopes. But its hand-written routes drop PATCH (405), and it adds redundant 201 handling and a tryFrom helper.

impl-1 ranks third. It is functionally solid, but it adds the 'web' middleware group (session plus CSRF) to the API routes. It also has a dead prepareForValidation trim, since TrimStrings already does that, and an awkward UpdatePostRequest-extends-StorePostRequest inheritance that redeclares almost every rule.

v.rationale:
All three share most of their design: enum status, #[Fillable]/#[ObservedBy]/#[Scope] attributes, an observer for the unique slug and published_at, a policy, FormRequests, JsonResource with tag names, and `latest()->latest('id')` pagination. All suites pass (impl-1: 20 tests, impl-2: 26, impl-3: 30). The ranking came down to what the probes found.

impl-3 ranks first. It authorizes with route `->can()` middleware, so non-authors get 403 before validation runs. That is the exact requirement, and it has a test. It also has the most complete tests. Its faults are minor: hand-written routes with no PATCH (405), a redundant setStatusCode(201), and a hand-rolled enum accessor.

impl-2 is the most idiomatic in its details: `$request->enum`, apiResource, slug route key, `distinct` validation and a composite index. But it calls Gate::authorize inside the action, after the FormRequest has validated. A non-author sending an invalid payload gets 422 instead of 403, which I confirmed with a probe. It also duplicates a postAttributes helper.

impl-1 shares impl-2's authorization-ordering issue and adds a more serious one. It puts API routes in the `web` group, and with CSRF enforced as in production, an authenticated JSON POST returned 419. It also has awkward FormRequest inheritance (`parent::rules()['status']`), trims tags by hand even though TrimStrings already does, confusing errors for null tags, and the thinnest test suite.

All three return 500 for a non-JSON guest request because no login route exists, so that issue doesn't affect the ranking.

v.rationale:
All three suites pass (26, 29 and 30 tests). They share the same core design: invokable controllers, a FormRequest that upper-cases the currency, after-commit observers using getPrevious(), and a lock plus last-known copy plus failure cooldown for the rates.

impl-1 ranks first. It is the only one to use Cache::flexible for the dashboard, which is the right fit for 'stale for up to 5 minutes if recomputing is slow'. Its lock wait is configurable, so the lock path is actually tested. Its validation (alpha:ascii) is strict, and every probe of the invalidation edge cases passed. Its main flaw is architectural: the API routes live in web.php.

impl-2 ranks second. Its code is clean, with a single observer and an api.php route file, but it uses Cache::remember with no stale-while-revalidate. Its lock wait is hardcoded and the lock path is untested, and a probe showed it caches an empty rates payload as fresh.

impl-3 ranks third. Its rates tests are strong, but probes confirmed real bugs: the exchange-rates endpoint wrongly requires auth, a currency with a trailing newline passes validation and reaches the API, and a stale loaded relation causes a missed invalidation when a task's project_id changes. It also uses remember instead of flexible, and its tests rely on $GLOBALS.

v.rationale: All three pass their own suites (impl-1 26, impl-2 29, impl-3 30), and they share a lot of structure. The ranking comes down to how closely each matched the caching brief and to the bugs the probes found. impl-1 is the only one that uses Cache::flexible([60,300]). That is the idiomatic answer to 'reflect changes within seconds, but serving stale data for up to 5 minutes is fine if recomputing is slow', and it combines it with after-commit observer invalidation that resolves teams by project_id. It also has the best stampede tests (a held lock, with and without last-known rates). Its weaknesses are API routes living in web.php (session cookies on API responses), exception-driven control flow around a broad RuntimeException, and no hook keeping completed_at in sync with status. impl-2 has the cleanest model and observer design and a completed_at hook, and its invalidation is correct, including moves. However, it uses plain remember (no stale-while-revalidate), has no lock-contention test, caches an empty rates payload as fresh, and adds 'web' middleware to api.php. impl-3 is almost identical to impl-2 but has a confirmed invalidation bug: it reads the possibly stale loaded $task->project relation, so the new team's dashboard is missed when a task moves. It also puts exchange-rates behind auth for no reason and uses $GLOBALS to swap fakes in its tests, which outweighs its nice timeout and re-entrancy tests. All three let lock waiters block for about 5s, beyond the 3s slow-API budget.

v.rationale: impl-1 is the most complete and idiomatic: the ownership check sits on the route, the queue settings use current attributes, the job is re-runnable, it handles the byte-order mark, and missing files and bad headers both record a clear reason. v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first, impl-1 second and impl-3 third. All three test suites pass (impl-1 and impl-2 have 25 tests each, impl-3 has 20).

**impl-2 (rank 1).** It is the only one with API auth that works for real clients: it installs Sanctum and uses `auth:sanctum`. It also has model attribute defaults, so the 202 response shows zero counts instead of nulls. Other strong points:
- modern queue attributes, including `WithoutRelations`
- batched error inserts
- route-level `->can()` authorization
- a missing file throws so the queue can retry
- the most thorough tests

Its real flaws:
- It doesn't strip the UTF-8 BOM, so an Excel 'CSV UTF-8' file fails the whole import (confirmed with a probe).
- `fgetcsv` is called without `escape`, which raises a PHP 8.4 deprecation on every row.

**impl-1 (rank 2) and impl-3 (rank 3)** share the most serious bug: `auth` (the session guard) on stateless API routes. Real API clients can never authenticate, and only `actingAs` in the tests gets past it. Both also return null counts in the POST response.

**Why impl-1 beats impl-3:**
- impl-1 throws a clear exception for a missing file, keeps the exception message in `failure_reason`, retries with Tries(3) and clears old row errors, and records original_name and started/finished timestamps.
- impl-1 authorizes with route `->can()` middleware and has a broader, well-split test suite.
- impl-3 hits a TypeError when the file is missing, replaces the failure reason with a generic message, and with Tries(1) plus its status guard it can never retry.
- impl-3 also has a factory without `user_id`, and one migration that creates two tables.
- impl-3 does have the nicest upload validation (`File::types()->max()`) and dispatches after commit, but that doesn't outweigh the problems above.

v.rationale: I ran the tests and read every added file for all three implementations. All three suites pass: impl-1 20 tests, impl-2 17, impl-3 18. In each implementation I probed a real permission-denied file on the local disk, and all three keep the row and exit with a failure code. impl-1 ranks first. It uses the framework's ConfirmableTrait and deletes in batches with chunkById plus partition, issuing one delete query per chunk, which is the most efficient approach on millions of rows. It rejects --days=0 and has the most complete tests, including retry on the next run and the interactive prompt. Its weaknesses are small: file deletes aren't wrapped in try/catch, which matters little because the disk has throw=false, and it uses a fixed 2h lock. impl-2 ranks second. It handles thrown delete exceptions, and its overlap protection is the strongest: a 6h lock plus withoutOverlapping. Its tests test the interactive prompt in-process. Against that, it writes its own confirmation instead of using ConfirmableTrait, deletes one row per query, and accepts --days=0, which purges everything. impl-3 ranks third. It is idiomatic in the command, using ConfirmableTrait, select plus lazyById, and catching delete failures. But it combines a 1h lock TTL with per-row deletes, so a long run on millions of rows can lose the lock and overlap. It also accepts --days=0, hardcodes a timezone nobody asked for, and its tests are weaker: hacky anonymous-class disk mocks, and a refusal test that never checks the prompt.

v.rationale:
All three have the same overall structure: a cutoff scope, dry-run before the confirmation, a cache lock with try/finally, a scheduled `--force` run on one server, and a local disk with throw=false. They differ in the details.

impl-1 has the most idiomatic and efficient purge loop: chunkById, then partition, then one bulk delete per chunk, plus ConfirmableTrait. It also has the most thorough tests, covering confirm yes and no, the non-interactive refusal and retry on the next run. Its weakness is that the file delete isn't wrapped in a try/catch. This only matters if the disk throws; the shipped config doesn't, but one setting change would make it stop at the first failure.

impl-2 handles failures most robustly (catches Throwable) and its operations are thorough: a 6h lock TTL plus withoutOverlapping. Its tests are solid. Against it: it hand-rolls the confirmation instead of using ConfirmableTrait, and it deletes one row per query.

impl-3 uses ConfirmableTrait and safe exception handling. It ranks last because of the short 1h lock TTL on a multi-million-row job with no schedule-level overlap guard, a hard-coded timezone nobody asked for, by-reference closure counters, brittle anonymous-class disk fakes, and no test that confirming 'yes' proceeds.

impl-1 and impl-2 are close. impl-1 edges ahead because its code and tests make better use of the framework.

- `?to=` without `from`

v.rationale:
All three use the same overall design: a readyToSync scope, claims written with toBase() so updated_at isn't touched, retryUntil below the 15-minute claim TTL, and failed() clearing claims. What separates them is how each behaves when the queue delivers a job more than once and when the API rate-limits.

**impl-2 (rank 1).** It is the only one that reads only rows that are still claimed, so a redelivered SQS job does nothing. It also handles Retry-After safely: values that aren't integers fall back to a default, and the wait is capped. It is the simplest of the three. Its remaining issues are narrow: an edit made in the same second after the read can be lost (impl-1 has the same window), and the endpoint is a hard-coded constant instead of config.

**impl-1 (rank 2).** It has the best test idioms (withFakeQueueInteractions, global preventStrayRequests) and adds withoutOverlapping. Its weaknesses:
- A duplicate delivery re-sends rows. The damage is limited, but one of its tests is named as if the job does nothing the second time while asserting it sent twice.
- It crashes with a TypeError when `missing` is null.
- It adds a RateLimited middleware with an invented limit, which is extra ceremony.

**impl-3 (rank 3).** It has a real bug: on a duplicate or late delivery, `synced_at = sync_started_at` becomes NULL, so rows are re-sent and the "exactly once per change" requirement is broken. Probes confirmed it. A Retry-After given as an HTTP date also makes it retry immediately while the API is still returning 429.

**Impl-1 (rank 1)** is the most correct.
- Order changes are conditional updates that only apply from allowed states, run in a transaction with a row lock. A repeated or late event can't move an order backwards (I checked this with a probe) and can't send a second receipt.
- The receipt is a queued notification sent only after the transaction commits.
- It handles 429 by waiting for the provider's Retry-After, and has the fullest README on running workers.
- Weaknesses: the cleanup is a hand-written command instead of the framework's prunable-model feature, the stuck-event recovery command goes beyond the brief, event types are string literals, and the tests use Mockery job mocks.

**Impl-3 (rank 2)** uses the cleanest framework features: prunable models, an `isFinal()` helper on the status enum, a queued notification with its own retry settings, and the newer fake-queue test helpers (`withFakeQueueInteractions`, `assertFailed`). But:
- A late `payment.failed` flips a paid order to payment_failed (I checked this).
- The "already paid" check has no lock, so two different events for the same payment running at once could both send a receipt.
- The Order and Refund factories crash on their own because they are missing required foreign keys.
- One migration is misnamed.

**Impl-2 (rank 3)** has the most real bugs, all confirmed with probes:
- The "processing" status is never saved, because only the attempts increment is written.
- Every `payment.succeeded` event sends a receipt, so a second event for the same payment sends a second one.
- The receipt is sent synchronously inside the job, and that step is not in a transaction with the order update.
- `payment.failed` overwrites a paid order.
- Its overlap lock has no release delay, so blocked jobs retry immediately and burn through the 50-try limit.
- Unknown event types are quietly marked processed.

Its prunable-model cleanup and route setup are good, but these bugs are in the task's main focus areas.

bugs: The 'processing' status is never saved: forceFill(['status' => Processing])->increment('attempts') only persists the incremented column, so after a 5xx the event stays 'pending' (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:51). Confirmed with a probe.

The PaymentReceipt notification is not queued and not after-commit (app/Notifications/PaymentReceipt.php:10), and the order update plus notify are not in a transaction, so the mail is sent inline inside the worker job.
If no order matches, the job fails permanently on the first attempt (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:81-84), so a webhook that arrives before its order row exists is lost without a retry.
An event with an empty data object ({}) is rejected with 422 by the 'required' array rule (PaymentWebhookRequest.php:14), which can cause endless provider redeliveries.

Tries(50) also counts RateLimited and WithoutOverlapping releases, and WithoutOverlapping uses the default releaseAfter(0), so under sustained throttling the job can run out of tries without hitting a real error.
antipatterns: Uses forceFill(...)->increment() and assumes the filled attributes are saved too (app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:51).
The admin API route lives in web.php behind session auth instead of routes/api.php (routes/web.php:16-18).
Unknown event types are silently marked processed with no record (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:53-55).
postWebhook test helper hand-builds HTTP_ server variables with collect()->mapWithKeys (tests/Pest.php:57-73) where withHeaders()->call() would do.
Tests the backoff by reflecting on attributes, which only asserts configuration (tests/Feature/ProcessWebhookEventTest.php:117-123).
strengths: The simplest implementation: createOrFirst on a unique event_id with dispatch only when wasRecentlyCreated, and a thin controller.
Uses MassPrunable with Schedule::command('model:prune') daily, plus queue:prune-failed.

Job configured with modern queue attributes (#[Tries, MaxExceptions, Backoff, Timeout, DeleteWhenMissingModels]) and the WithoutOverlapping and RateLimited middleware with a shared perSecond(10) limiter.
Refunds are idempotent through a unique webhook_event_id with firstOrCreate inside a transaction; 4xx fails permanently and 5xx/429 retry.

Pest tests use a global beforeEach with Http::preventStrayRequests, datasets, and lock/rate-limit behaviour tests.

bugs: An unauthenticated GET /api/webhook-events without Accept: application/json returns 500 because route [login] is not defined (routes/web.php:16-18, bootstrap/app.php). Confirmed with a probe.

OrderFactory has no user_id, so Order::factory()->create() throws a NOT NULL violation and every caller must chain ->for($user) (database/factories/OrderFactory.php:14-22); RefundFactory likewise has no order or webhook_event.

PaymentProviderClient::payment() declares an array return type, so a 200 response with an empty body throws TypeError (app/Services/PaymentProviderClient.php:17-25). It is then retried as a generic exception.
retryUntil is fixed at 2 hours from dispatch, so a backlog longer than that fails jobs without processing them (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:47-50).
If no order matches, the job fails permanently with no retry (ProcessWebhookEvent.php:71-75), so an out-of-order delivery is lost.
antipatterns: The migration is named create_orders_table but also creates webhook_events and refunds (database/migrations/2026_11_07_000002_create_orders_table.php).
The README section is inserted into the untouched Laravel boilerplate (README.md).
Global const declarations in Pest test files (PAYMENT_URL, SECRET) can collide across files (tests/Feature/ProcessWebhookEventTest.php:21, tests/Feature/ReceiveWebhookTest.php:8).
The admin API route lives in web.php with session auth (routes/web.php:16).
The StoreWebhookEvent action class is a small extra layer for what amounts to createOrFirst plus dispatch (app/Actions/StoreWebhookEvent.php).
strengths: Receipt is a ShouldQueueAfterCommit notification with its own Tries/Backoff attributes, sent from inside a DB::transaction, and skipped when the order is already paid, so the receipt is never sent twice.
Job uses retryUntil together with MaxExceptions(5) and Backoff([5,30,120,600]), so middleware releases do not burn the retry budget; this is documented clearly.
WithoutOverlapping keyed by event_id with releaseAfter(15)/expireAfter(120), plus the RateLimited middleware and a shared Limit::perSecond(10).
Deletes the stored event if dispatch throws, so the provider's redelivery is not swallowed as a duplicate.
Uses MassPrunable with a daily model:prune, isFinal() on the status enum, a scopeWithStatus scope, and typed status()/perPage() accessors on the FormRequest.
Tests use withFakeQueueInteractions()->assertFailed(), datasets, Http::sequence, and include an end-to-end sync-queue test (38 tests).

v.rationale: All three pass their own suites (impl-2: 34 tests, impl-3: 38, impl-1: 42). All three share the same core: createOrFirst on a unique event_id, a job using the WithoutOverlapping and RateLimited middleware with a perSecond(10) limiter, failed() writing the error to the event, and a policy-gated index with a FormRequest. impl-3 ranks first: it covers the focus area most completely (an after-commit queued receipt sent inside a transaction and never twice, retryUntil plus MaxExceptions so releases don't burn tries, cleanup if dispatch fails, model:prune). Its bugs are peripheral: a 500 for unauthenticated non-JSON requests, a broken OrderFactory default, and a boilerplate README. impl-2 is the simplest and cleanest, and the only one returning 401 instead of 500 for guests. But its 'processing' status is never saved (forceFill + increment), its receipt is neither queued nor after-commit, and Tries(50) can be used up by throttle releases. impl-1 is the most defensive (status-guarded transitions, lockForUpdate, 429 Retry-After). It falls short on idioms: a hand-written prune command instead of Prunable, an extra stuck-event recovery command, string-literal event types, Mockery job mocks, and a hardcoded EUR currency. It also shares the 500-on-guest bug.
